props.title: A composite action, inside your repo

notes.t: run steps in a composite must set shell

captions: Part five. The actions themselves.

Workflows stay short because of reuse. Let's see
how.
An action is a packaged, reusable step.

The GitHub Marketplace lists thousands of them.
Checking out
code. Setting up Node, Python, Java or Go. Caching.

Uploading artifacts. Building Docker images. Logging
in to AWS,
Azure or Google Cloud.

You reference one with uses: the owner, the
repository,
and after the at sign, a version.
That version can be a tag like v4, a
branch, or a full commit hash.
Remember that detail. It matters a lot in the
security chapter.
You can write your own actions, in three flavors.
A JavaScript action runs directly on the runner with

Node. It starts fastest, and works on every
operating
system.

A Docker container action ships its own environment.
Fully
reproducible, but Linux only, and slower to start.
A composite action is simply a bundle of steps,
packaged as one. It's the easiest to write.
All three are described by a file called action
dot yml, which declares the inputs, the outputs, and
how to run.

Here's a composite action, living inside the
repository.
It declares one input, the node version, with a
default.

Under runs, using composite, it lists ordinary
steps: set
up Node with caching, then install dependencies.
Note that run steps inside a composite must declare
a shell.
Now every workflow in this repo can replace those
steps with a single line: uses, dot slash, dot
github, slash actions, slash setup app.
For bigger reuse, there are reusable workflows.
A workflow whose trigger is workflow call can be

called by other workflows — even from other
repositories.
It takes inputs and secrets, and runs whole jobs.

Platform teams love this. Write one hardened deploy
pipeline,
and fifty services call it. Fix a bug once,
and everyone gets the fix.

Rule of thumb: composite actions reuse steps.
Reusable workflows
reuse jobs.
Since late twenty twenty five, you can nest reusable
workflows ten levels deep, and call up to fifty
in one run.
